name: Mozilla Readability (readability.js). Aliases: @mozilla/readability, the Firefox Reader View engine. Ports/derivatives: readability-lxml (Python), go-readability, dom-smoothie (JS), and the Readability gold-standard dataset named after it.
kind: Library (JavaScript, operates on a parsed DOM Document) that is also shipped as a browser feature inside Firefox Reader View.
maturity: Production, actively maintained by Mozilla; the de facto baseline every other extractor is compared against. The algorithm itself is largely frozen; changes are threshold and regex tuning.
license: Apache-2.0. Permits use in this project without restriction, including redistribution and modification.
keeps_and_discards: Scores block-level nodes with a hand-tuned heuristic: class/id regex matches (unlikelyCandidates covering banner, combx, comment, community, disqus, extra, footer, header, menu, sidebar, sponsor, share, social; positive covering article, body, content, entry, main, page, post, text), comma counts, text length, and link density. It keeps the top-scoring candidate subtree plus siblings above a fraction of the top score, and discards navigation, footers, comment threads, ad rails, and almost all forms and controls. Output is a sanitized HTML fragment plus title, byline, excerpt, siteName, lang and publishedTime. It explicitly refuses non-article pages via the isProbablyReaderable gate and a charThreshold (default 500 characters), so a listing, product or forum page either returns null or returns an arbitrary fragment. Everything that is not prose in one contiguous container is gone by construction.
structure_preserved: Inside the chosen subtree, heading/paragraph/list/table/blockquote nesting and document order survive, and the result is reserialized into a flat wrapper div (readability-page-1) so the original ancestor chain above the candidate is destroyed. Layout tables are unwrapped; data tables survive as HTML. Everything outside the candidate subtree loses all structural relation to what is kept -- there is no record that a discarded nav ever sat as a sibling. Shadow boundaries are not handled at all: Readability walks a light-DOM document, so open shadow roots are invisible unless the caller pre-flattens them, and there is no unreachable marker for what it did not see. Tabular relations survive only within the kept fragment; cross-container relations (a caption in one div, its figure in another) are frequently severed.
interactive_elements: Removed. The _clean pass strips form, input, button, select, textarea, object, embed, and iframe (with an allowlist for recognised video embeds). Anchors survive as <a href> with resolved absolute URLs, but that is the only affordance that lives through the pass, and it carries no state.
interactive_state_fidelity: Effectively zero, and structurally so rather than incidentally. disabled, checked, selected, aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-pressed and role are not preserved because the elements carrying them are deleted before serialization. aria-* is consulted only negatively: aria-hidden and the hidden attribute are used to skip nodes, and role appears in the unlikely-candidate regex. The token cost of interactive state is therefore nil, but so is the affordance count, which makes Readability the extreme prose-only endpoint of the axis: it is the control that shows what a fold gives up when it optimises for reading rather than for acting. For a sensor whose output must let a model click something, Readability is a negative oracle, not a design.
layout_awareness: Almost none, and none geometric. There is no getBoundingClientRect, no computed-style cascade read, no viewport notion. The one exception is _isProbablyVisible, which checks the inline style attribute for display:none / visibility:hidden, the hidden attribute, and aria-hidden. Against a live DOM this reads declared style; against parsed HTML it reads only the attribute. So it reads a small amount of declared style and no geometry.
javascript_required: Not by the library, which is a pure function over an already-parsed Document. But the input's provenance decides everything: Firefox Reader View runs after load, so the page's scripts (and its analytics) have already fired; the standalone library run over raw fetched HTML sees only server-rendered markup and returns the loading skeleton for client-rendered pages. Readability itself fires no telemetry and makes no requests.
evaluation_method: Mozilla publishes no fidelity metric. Correctness is enforced by a regression fixture set: test/test-pages/ holds saved source pages each paired with an expected-output HTML and expected-metadata JSON, and CI asserts byte-level agreement. That is a change-detector, not a measurement -- when a threshold is retuned, the expected outputs are regenerated. All quantitative figures in circulation come from third parties: CleanEval, Bevendorff et al. (SIGIR 2023), the SIGIR 2025 multilingual study, and WCXB (2026).
corpus_size_and_origins: Mozilla's own: roughly 180 archived pages accumulated ad hoc from bug reports over about a decade, overwhelmingly English news and blogs, with no published origin count and no sampling frame -- it is a bug-report residue, not a sample of the web. External corpora that carry the numbers: CleanEval, 684 English plus 653 Chinese pages downloaded in 2006 (published 2007); CleanPortalEval, ~70 pages from 4 news portals; L3S-GN1, 621 Google News pages (2010); WCXB, 2,008 pages from 1,613 domains collected September 2025 to March 2026, median 1 page per domain. The generation gap matters: the corpus that made Readability's reputation predates responsive layout, SPAs, consent banners and shadow DOM entirely.
reported_precision_recall: WCXB word-bag F1 (development set, 1,497 pages): 0.674 overall; by type, article 0.897, documentation 0.789, service 0.744, forum 0.685, listing 0.631, product 0.596, collection 0.547. The denominator is a bag of lowercased word tokens against an LLM-drafted, human-adjudicated main-content span, so word order is not scored. Trafilatura's own benchmark (990 documents, 2,951 text and 2,966 boilerplate segments, run 2026-08-04) scores readability-lxml well below trafilatura, but that ranking is produced by a competitor. Note an unresolved arithmetic oddity: WCXB's 0.674 aggregate sits below six of its seven per-type scores, which implies the aggregate is page-weighted over a distribution including null returns rather than a mean of the type scores.
independent_oracle: No genuinely independent one exists. WCXB, Bevendorff et al. and the multilingual study all evaluate Readability without Mozilla, but every one of them scores against a human- or LLM-drawn main-content span -- the same object Readability's heuristic is a guess at. The oracle and the tool share the premise that a page has one contiguous main content. On a listing or a product page that premise is false, and the measured 0.547 is partly the oracle's disagreement with itself. The only assumption-free checks available are oracle-free ones (round-trip fixed point, recall against the raw capture), and nobody has published those for Readability.
evidence_independence: Mozilla has never published a fidelity figure, so no number attributed to Readability is vendor-run. Every circulating number is instead COMPETITOR-run: WCXB was authored by Murrough Foley, who also wrote rs-trafilatura, the system that tops that benchmark; Bevendorff et al. (SIGIR 2023) are the Webis/ChatNoir group who wrote Resiliparse; Trafilatura's published table is run by Trafilatura's author. The SIGIR 2025 multilingual study (GREYC, Universite de Caen Normandie) is the only comparison in this area with no horse in the race. This is the inverse of the vendor-bias problem, not an escape from it, and Readability's figures should be read as lower bounds set by interested parties.
page_archetype_coverage: A 35-point spread in WCXB, 0.897 on articles down to 0.547 on collections, so any single aggregate is misleading. The spread is not a tuning failure -- isProbablyReaderable is an explicit refusal to handle non-article pages, so on listings, products and collections the tool is being scored outside its declared domain. WCXB's own finding that article extraction is largely solved (every top system between 0.87 and 0.93) means Readability is competitive exactly where the task is easy and collapses exactly where a general-purpose sensor has to work.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Not script-invariant. Length gates are character counts (charThreshold 500, plus per-paragraph minimums), which systematically penalise CJK because a Chinese paragraph carries far more information per character than an English one -- a CJK page must be substantially longer in content terms to clear the same gate. The comma heuristic was patched to count the full-width CJK comma, which is an admission that the feature was language-specific. There is no bidi handling, no RTL-specific behaviour and no bidi isolation on output, so mixed-direction text is reserialized without isolation marks. The SIGIR 2025 multilingual study finds Chinese the hardest of its five settings for all extractors, Greek the easiest.
leaks_outward: Nothing, as a library: it performs no network I/O, reads no storage, and emits no telemetry. The disclosure risk is entirely in how it is fed. The common server-side pattern (fetch the URL again, then distil) discloses a second, session-less fetch to the origin and to any CDN in front of it, with a different IP, UA and TLS fingerprint than the user's browser -- a linkable signal that the page is being processed. Inside Firefox, entering Reader View is a local action but the distillation path re-loads the document, which the origin can observe as a second request.
mechanism_detectability: As a library over exported HTML, undetectable -- there is nothing for the page to observe. In-browser Reader View is partially detectable: the distilled document is a separate about:reader page whose scripts do not run, so an origin that ships a beacon in the article body will see the beacon stop firing while the user is still reading, and the re-load pattern is visible server-side. Readability does not patch any DOM API, does not use CDP, and does not touch attachShadow, so it introduces none of the detectability signals this project refuses.
countermeasures: None are needed for the library. Hardening is one-sided in practice: sites counter Readability at the content level with paywall stubs that distil cleanly into a teaser presented as the article, decoy containers carrying the positive class regex, and bodies lazy-loaded after scroll so the distiller sees an empty candidate. There is no signature to hide, so there is nothing to harden against detection.
measured_fidelity_cost: Unmeasured. Mozilla publishes no figure for what distillation costs relative to the full page, and no third party frames the loss as a hardening cost against a stated control. WCXB's with-snippet versus without-snippet split is the nearest proxy -- it separates completeness from boilerplate contamination -- but the control there is a human-drawn span, not a full capture, so the number that matters to this project (affordances retained versus affordances present) has never been computed for Readability. Given that it deletes every form control, the affordance retention rate would be near zero against a 99.7% capture baseline.
gate_state_at_capture: Not recorded and not representable. Readability has no notion of consent banners, paywalls, login walls or CAPTCHA interstitials; it will distil a paywall teaser and return it as the article with no flag, and it will distil a consent-wall body if that body scores highest. Since roughly two thirds of top sites present a consent interface, a Readability-built corpus silently mixes gated and ungated captures with no field to separate them afterwards. This is the single most corpus-poisoning property of the tool.
determinism: Deterministic for a fixed input document, fixed version and fixed parser: pure computation, no randomness, no clock, no network. One sharp caveat -- it mutates the input Document in place, so the caller must clone; running it twice on the same live document is not idempotent and the second run returns a degraded or null result. Same input, same output holds only if input means a pristine copy.
determinism_across_versions: Output drifts materially between releases. The class/id regexes, the sibling-inclusion fraction, charThreshold and the retry-with-relaxed-flags ladder are retuned continuously, and the committed expected-output fixtures are regenerated when they are. Output also drifts with the host parser: JSDOM, live Gecko, and the lxml/Go ports differ on entity handling, whitespace normalisation, implied tbody insertion and inline-style parsing, so the same HTML through readability-lxml and @mozilla/readability is not the same text. Pinning both library version and parser is mandatory.
reproducibility: High if (library version, parser, input bytes) are pinned, and the fixture corpus makes that achievable. Low in practice, because the normal input is a live fetch of a page that changes under you -- which is exactly the failure this project already has with 75% of its corpus fetching live resources on every read. Readability offers no help here: it records nothing about what it read.
failure_modes: Five distinct ones, in rough order of frequency. (1) Wrong subtree returned with full confidence -- a comment thread, a related-articles rail, or a single pull-quote scores highest and is returned as the article. (2) Truncation, where an article split across sibling containers loses its tail because the sibling-inclusion threshold rejects the continuation. (3) Silent element loss: tables, figures, code blocks and pre-formatted content stripped by _clean because their link density or class name matched. (4) Null return when nothing clears charThreshold, common on SPAs and short pages. (5) Skeleton capture, where a client-rendered page yields a loading placeholder. Only (4) is a loud failure.
failure_visibility: Mostly silent, and silent in the dominant case. A null return is loud and easy to branch on, but the wrong-subtree and truncation failures are indistinguishable from success in the output: there is no confidence score, no candidate-margin field, no count of discarded nodes, no indication that the second-place candidate scored within one percent of the winner. A pipeline built on Readability cannot tell a good extraction from a bad one without an external check, which is exactly the silent-degradation pattern this project refuses.
scale_limits: Linear in node count with a constant of several full-document passes, and _grabArticle can re-run up to four times with progressively relaxed flags, so pathological pages cost roughly four traversals. It is whole-document in memory with no streaming, so cost tracks DOM size, not content size -- a 50k-node page of mostly chrome costs as much as a 50k-node page of prose. There is no batch amortisation and no incremental mode, so cost is strictly per page and never sublinear across a corpus.
delta_cost_model: There is none, and this is disqualifying rather than merely absent. Readability is whole-document by construction: the scores are computed from global statistics (top-candidate score, sibling threshold as a fraction of it), so a one-character text change can flip which subtree wins and there is no local recomputation that would detect this. Cost is O(page) for every change, and every class of change falls outside any delta bound -- text edits, attribute changes, subtree insertion, and shadow mutations alike. It is the direct negation of the O(delta) constraint, and useful only as the worst-case control against which a delta claim is measured.
reanchoring_stability: No node identity exists at any point. The output fragment carries no xpath, no source-node ids (ids are stripped by the sanitizer), no character offsets into the source, and no content hashes. There is therefore no re-anchoring, no re-anchor rate to measure, and no way to diff two runs beyond text diffing the results -- which conflates a DOM move with a content change. Compared with W3C Web Annotation dual selectors or CDC boundaries, Readability sits at the floor: it discards the address space entirely.
adversarial_exposure: Partially exposed, and exposed in the band that matters. It removes inline display:none, the hidden attribute and aria-hidden, which catches naive concealment. It does not read computed style, so text hidden by an external stylesheet class, positioned off-screen with absolute coordinates, clipped to zero height, given a zero font-size, or coloured to match the background survives into the output if it sits inside the winning subtree. Its accidental defence is deletion volume: it throws away so much of the page that most injected payloads are discarded as boilerplate. That is a coverage artefact, not a filter, and it inverts on a payload placed inside the article body. It cannot filter concealment without reading layout, and it does not read layout -- the same structural exposure this project has, with less capture to compensate.
provenance_carrying: None per token, and effectively none per document. The output object carries a title, byline, excerpt, siteName, lang and publishedTime scraped from the page's own metadata -- which is attacker-controlled -- and nothing about the read itself. No url (documentURI is an input used only to resolve relative links, not an output), no xpath, no capture timestamp, no shadow depth, no gate state, no version stamp. Provenance can only be bolted on at whole-document granularity by the caller, which is too coarse for the per-token origin that current injection defences require and that this project's url:xpath:markdown:content trie key already supplies for free.
roundtrip_safety: Not a fixed point. Feeding Readability's own output back into Readability yields a different result, usually a smaller fragment or a null, because the output has been stripped of the class names, sibling context and link-density contrasts that the scorer needs -- the transform destroys its own input signal. The escaping policy is an HTML allowlist inside _clean, and Mozilla is explicit that it is not an XSS sanitizer and that DOMPurify must be run separately; script, style, and event-handler attributes are removed but the guarantee is not stated as security-grade. Any markdown serialization is a separate downstream step with its own, unrelated escaping policy.
token_budget_and_ordering: There is no budget concept and no ordering contract. Output is source order of the winning subtree, nothing is truncated by the library (charThreshold only decides whether it returns at all), and there is no notion of which content is highest value. Where the important content lands in a model's context is therefore whatever the page's author decided, which past the 50% context fill point -- where position bias turns recency-dominant -- means the ordering is uncontrolled. If Readability output is used as SLM context, the caller owns the entire ordering problem; the library contributes nothing but a smaller haystack.
representation_cost: Typically 5-20% of the source HTML's token count on an article, and effectively a total loss on anything else. What is bought per token saved: all interactive affordances, all interactive state, all provenance, all addressability, and the entire non-article surface of the page. The compression is real and large, but it is achieved by deletion rather than by encoding, so the ratio cannot be traded back against fidelity -- there is no dial that recovers what was dropped.
what_could_be_adopted: Three specific mechanisms, none of them the algorithm. (1) _isProbablyVisible as a cheap non-geometric visibility predicate -- inline style display/visibility, the hidden attribute, aria-hidden -- which is legal inside the fold because it reads declared attributes rather than computed geometry, and which closes the naive slice of the concealed-content gap at near-zero cost. (2) Link density (anchor text characters over total text characters) as a structure-agnostic per-node scalar: it names no region, requires no page-structure prior, is computable incrementally as a node's text changes, and can ride on the trie as a peripheral rather than as a classifier. (3) The regression-fixture discipline itself: a pinned set of saved pages with committed expected outputs is precisely the frozen control this project lacks while 75% of its 136-page corpus refetches live resources, and it is cheap to build.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: REJECTED. The unlikelyCandidates/positive/negative class-and-id regexes are literally a classifier naming regions nav, sidebar, footer, comment and article. This is the constraint's paradigm violation, not a borderline case. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS. No geometry is read; _isProbablyVisible reads declared style and the hidden/aria-hidden attributes, which is address-local metadata, not layout. o_delta: REJECTED. Whole-document global scoring with no local recomputation path; a one-character change can flip the winning subtree. no_mocks: NEUTRAL, adoptable as-is. It is a pure DOM transform with no stub surface; it neither helps nor hinders the real-browser requirement. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY. It never touches attachShadow so it does not violate the rule, but it also never traverses shadow roots and emits no unreachable marker, so it silently under-reports shadow content -- exactly the dishonest-coverage behaviour the constraint exists to prevent. OVERALL: negative oracle only, with two mechanisms (visibility predicate, link density) extractable as-is.
governance_signal_handling: None whatsoever. Readability is a transform with no fetcher, so it reads no robots.txt, honours no Content Signals or ai.txt directive, implements no IETF AIPREF vocabulary, presents no Web Bot Auth signature or Signature Agent Card, and has no HTTP 402 path. Every governance obligation falls on whatever performs the fetch. For this project that is the browser under the user's own session, which is the favourable case, but it also means adopting Readability contributes nothing to a governance story and cannot be cited as compliance.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: As a transform it retains nothing; the caller's persisted artifact is the regulated act under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026. What it hands the caller to persist is unhelpful: it retains bylines and author names as first-class metadata fields, keeps any PII inside the article body verbatim, and frequently keeps comment-thread text it misclassified as content -- user-generated content with a materially different expectation of privacy than editorial copy. It performs no redaction, carries no gate-state marker, and records no capture time, so a legitimate-interest balancing test over a Readability-built store has no data to work from and the data-minimisation argument has to be made entirely outside the tool.
